articles.title: HAL, Safran seal engine deal to power multi-role choppers
articles.summary: News News: BENGALURU: Defence PSU HAL and Safran Helicopter Engines have signed the final contract with their joint venture, Safhal Helicopter Engines Pvt Ltd, t.
articles.body: BENGALURU: Defence PSU HAL and Safran Helicopter Engines have signed the final contract with their joint venture, Safhal Helicopter Engines Pvt Ltd, to design and develop a new high-power helicopter engine that will power Indiaâs proposed 13-tonne Indian Multi-Role Helicopter (IMRH) and its naval variant Deck-Based Multi-Role Helicopter (DBMRH).The engine, Aravalli, named after Indiaâs iconic mountain range, will be developed in the 3,500-4,000 shaft horsepower (shp) class. The contract covers its design, development, manufacture, supply and lifecycle support.The agreement was signed by HALâs director (engineering and R&D) Ajay Kumar Shrivastava and Olivier Savin, director, Safhal Helicopter Engines and executive vice-president (sales and marketing) at Safran Helicopter Engines.âThe signing of this contract marks a significant step forward in Indiaâs pursuit of self-reliance in aero-engine technologies. Through this collaborative programme with Safhal and Safran Helicopter Engines, weâre creating a strong foundation for powering next-generation Indian helicopter platforms,â HAL CMD Ravi K said.Aravalli will be a new-generation turboshaft engine designed specifically for the IMRH and DBMRH. Safran Helicopter Engines chief executive Cedric Goubet said the programme marked a new phase in the partnership between the two companies.âThis is the first time Safran HE has taken up such a class of engine as co-development. The Aravalli engine programme represents a new chapter in the strategic relationship between France and India, combining the expertise of our teams to develop propulsion systems for future Indian rotorcraft,â Goubet said.HAL and Safran have worked together on helicopter engines for decades. Safranâs Artouste engines powered the Cheetah and Chetak helicopters, while the Shakti engine family powers HALâs Advanced Light Helicopter, Light Combat Helicopter and Light Utility Helicopter.Beyond the two military helicopter programmes â IMRH and DBMRH â Aravalli could also find applications in civil aviation, including offshore transport, utility missions and VVIP travel. The programme is also expected to support the development of maintenance, repair and overhaul capabilities in India.The IMRH programme is central to HALâs plans to develop a medium-lift helicopter to meet the requirements of the Indian armed forces, potentially replacing ageing platforms and reducing dependence on imported helicopters and engines.

articles.title: Far-right Israeli lawmaker damages Palestinian memorial with sledgehammer
articles.summary: Zvi Sukkot's actions have drawn widespread condemnation, including from Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu.
articles.body:
A far-right member of the Israeli parliament has badly damaged a Palestinian memorial with a sledgehammer in the occupied West Bank while under military escort.

The incident has drawn strong criticism from Palestinians and across the political spectrum in Israel.

Video footage showed Zvi Sukkot, a member of the far-right Religious Zionism party, and several others striking the stone memorial in the Palestinian village of Madama.

In the video, Sukkot - who has a history of provocative anti-Palestinian acts - says: "This is something we cannot leave standing here, because any place that glorifies terrorism, we must remove it."

Rami Nasar, the head of the village council in Madama, said that the monument was erected in 2008 to remember Palestinians killed in the battle of Karameh - a day-long military confrontation between Israeli forces and those of both the PLO and Jordan in 1968.

It also memorialises Palestinians killed in the first and second intifada.

Nasar said it was intended to honour those who had been killed in conflict with Israel, whatever their political affiliation.

The Israel Defense Forces (IDF) said its soldiers had been present during the incident. The Israeli military said it had approved a tour of monuments in the area for Sukkot and was providing security.

But the IDF said he and the others involved had acted deceptively and without authorisation.

It said soldiers eventually stopped Sukkot and escorted his group out of Madama after reporting the incident to their commanders.

In a number of previous incidents involving settler violence, soldiers have been filmed standing by without intervening.

The incident has further raised the temperature in the West Bank, where increasing attacks by settlers on Palestinians in recent months have drawn international condemnation.

Madama itself has been the target of several attacks by settlers.

Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's office has issued a statement criticising Sukkot's actions. It read: "Taking the law into one's own hands, especially when it involves public figures, is a reprehensible practice that prevents the IDF from focusing on its missions of combating terrorism and incitement to violence."

Netanyahu's main rival in the upcoming general election, Gadi Eisenkot, said that Sukkot's behaviour was "a disgrace for anyone who claims to represent the public and be a leader".

Eisenkot also criticised Netanyahu for "allowing anarchists like Zvi Sukkot and his ilk to do whatever they please, endangering security in the settlements and harming Israel's standing in the world".

But finance minister Bezalel Smotrich - who heads the Religious Zionism party to which Sukkot belongs - directed his fiercest criticism at what he called the "frantic rush of the left-wing opposition to condemn Sukkot rather than terrorism itself".

On Monday, the most senior Israeli military officer in the West Bank, Major General Avi Bluth, was reported by Israeli media to have told Netanyahu in a closed-door meeting that the mounting violence by settlers could ignite a major escalation.

articles.title: Trump’s Korean gambit exposes a shifting East Asian order
articles.summary: Growing doubts about the US security umbrella are forcing new strategic calculations across the region.
articles.body:
When President Donald Trump ordered the Pentagon to cut the annual United States-South Korea Ulchi Freedom Shield (UFS) military exercise planned for mid-August from 11 days to five, he laid bare the transactional logic of his approach to East Asia. The move blindsided Seoul and drew a calculated rebuff from Pyongyang, underscoring how growing doubts about the US defence umbrella are reshaping strategic calculations across the region.

Trump framed the reduction as a goodwill gesture towards Kim Jong Un, whom he described as a leader he “knows very well” and with whom he has a “very good relationship”. He claimed the drills sent a “totally inappropriate and hostile” signal to Pyongyang and linked the decision directly to Seoul’s refusal to join the US war effort in Iran, declaring that America “can’t go around and protect all of these countries, especially when they’re not there to help us”.

Pyongyang’s response to Trump’s overture was carefully calibrated. Kim Yo Jong, Kim Jong Un’s sister, stated she was “unaware” of any communication between the two leaders, contradicting Trump’s claim of a “very positive” exchange. Yet she reaffirmed her brother’s “personally good memories and feelings” towards the US president, signalling that Pyongyang remains open to engagement, but on very different terms: Washington would have to accept North Korea as a nuclear-armed state and abandon what Pyongyang calls its “hostile” policy. Those demands remain fundamentally at odds with Washington’s insistence on complete denuclearisation, raising the prospect that any November meeting could amount to little more than political theatre unless one side changes its position.

China’s response to the renewed prospect of US-North Korea engagement was more restrained, but no less revealing. Beijing was more circumspect about the prospect. Foreign Ministry Spokesperson Lin Jian declined to comment on a possible Trump-Kim meeting. China’s broader position, however, emerged more clearly when Foreign Minister Wang Yi visited Seoul. He urged South Korea to pursue“genuine strategic autonomy” and avoid “bloc confrontation or taking sides”, while calling for accelerated negotiations on the second phase of the China-South Korea Free Trade Agreement and expanded cooperation in AI, the green transition and the digital economy. More significantly, Wang made no reference to denuclearisation and did not endorse Seoul’s multiparty peace initiative, instead speaking of “peaceful coexistence” on the peninsula. The formulation appears to move Beijing closer to accepting the reality of two separate Korean states, rather than continuing to centre denuclearisation as the organising principle of peninsula diplomacy. Notably, Washington appears to be moving in parallel: in the August 25 readout of the Cho Hyun–Marco Rubio call, the US State Department conspicuously omitted any reference to denuclearisation — a term that had appeared routinely in previous trilateral statements as recently as July 22.

Wang also warned against “Japanese right-wing forces’ attempts to reverse the course of history”, urging that “Japanese militarism never be allowed to rise again”. His warning points directly to the speed and scale of Tokyo’s military transformation. Japan under Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi is moving rapidly to entrench that process. Trump’s latest move did not start this, but it reinforces the logic behind greater Japanese strategic autonomy. On July 31, Tokyo inaugurated its National Intelligence Bureau, strengthening the prime minister’s control over intelligence coordination across government. Japan’s core defence budget has reached a record 9.04 trillion yen ($56.7bn), while Japan says broader defence-related spending has reached its benchmark of 2 percent of gross domestic product ahead of schedule. The buildup is also being embedded in fiscal policy through new defence-related taxes. The pace of this shift has drawn Pyongyang’s wrath: Kim Yo-jong warned Japan that any “wrong choice” would bring “an immediate and unsurvivable, annihilating strike”.

For Beijing, however, the deeper concern is the autonomy of Tokyo’s drive. Japan is seizing the uncertainty surrounding Washington’s commitments to institutionalise military normalisation. Relaxed weapons export rules and deepening symbiosis with defence contractors Mitsubishi Heavy Industries, Kawasaki Heavy Industries and IHI, whose combined defence order backlogs reach 6.25 trillion yen ($39.2bn), signal a Japan building the institutional scaffolding for greater independent action. For Beijing, this is the nightmare scenario: A rapidly remilitarised Japan operating not merely as a US proxy, but as an independent great power asserting its own sphere of influence as US credibility frays.

Seoul, too, is recalibrating. On August 18, after Trump ordered the UFS cut, President Lee Jae Myung renewed his push to regain wartime operational control of South Korean forces and accelerate plans for nuclear-powered submarines, arguing that stronger independent defence capabilities should complement the US alliance.

At the centre of this emerging order is a geopolitical triangle: A US treating alliances as transactional commodities, a Japan racing towards permanent military emancipation amid growing uncertainty over US commitments, and a China stabilising its periphery while pushing back against Tokyo’s rightward turn. South Korea, caught in the middle, is increasingly forced to navigate Washington’s unpredictability, Beijing’s economic gravity, and Tokyo’s accelerating militarism.

The uncertainty is profound. If Trump’s rapprochement with Pyongyang produces only theatre, North Korea’s nuclear programme will continue to advance as Beijing and Moscow shield Pyongyang from meaningful external pressure. If Washington’s pressure on Seoul succeeds, South Korea may be dragged deeper into America’s wars, from the Strait of Hormuz to a Taiwan contingency. If Tokyo’s remilitarisation proceeds unchecked, the post-war regional security architecture could be irrevocably altered.

The APEC summit in Shenzhen this November may offer the first real diplomatic test of this emerging order. The prospect of Trump, Xi Jinping, the Japanese and South Korean leaders, and possibly Kim Jong Un converging in one Chinese city would give Beijing an unusually prominent opportunity to shape the diplomatic response to this disorder. Whether it can broker a stabilising understanding, or the summit becomes another stage for competing nationalisms, could help determine East Asia’s trajectory for the decade to come.

The old certainties are eroding. The US alliance system that has anchored the region for three-quarters of a century is being weakened from within. Japan is exploiting the resulting ambiguity to shed post-war constraints. China, preferring a stable periphery and appearing increasingly willing to accommodate a permanent two-state reality on the peninsula, finds itself managing a level of regional uncertainty not seen since the Cold War.

No single summit can arrest the forces driving this transformation. East Asia is entering a new order in which Washington’s ability to set the terms is diminishing, its allies are testing the limits of their dependence, and its rivals are seeking to shape what comes next.

The views expressed in this article are the author’s own and do not necessarily reflect Al Jazeera’s editorial stance.

articles.title: In 1978, Seoul began dumping its rubbish on a river island; 15 years and 92 million cubic metres of waste later, two 98-metre garbage mountains were sealed beneath five ecological parks
articles.summary: Rest of World News: Discover how Nanjido Island in Seoul transformed from a massive landfill into a beautiful ecological park featuring hiking trails and green spaces, following years of waste disposal and remediation efforts.
articles.body: For fifteen years, a small island on the Han River took in almost everything Seoul threw away. By the time the dumping stopped, the site held two mounds of trash nearly a hundred metres tall. What happened next was a slow process of sealing, planting and rebuilding that transformed one of the cityâs most notorious eyesores into a cluster of public parks with football stadiums, hiking trails and silver grass festivals.1978: Nanjido was chosen after Seoul's existing dump sites reached capacity Waste generation in Seoul in the 1970s was outstripping the capacity of existing waste disposal sites. For instance, areas such as Gunja-dong, Sangwolgok-dong and Yeomchang-dong, which have been dumping grounds since 1964, were becoming overcrowded due to the increased population and construction in Seoul. The government sought a site that would be easily accessible by transportation and chose Nanjido Island in the Han River, where wild orchids used to grow. The research on this history, A Study on the Current Status of Landfill in Seoul and the Solutions to Future Generation Landfill Problems, published in the Journal of Wellbeing Management and Applied Psychology, records that dumping at Nanjido ran from March 1978 to March 1993. During this period, Nanjido served as Seoul's primary waste disposal site, though independent verification of the city's exact population served or the precise share of household waste processed was not available.March 1978 to March 1993: 92 million cubic metres dumped to create two 98 metre high moundsNanjido landfill differed from sanitary landfills of today in not being lined, covered, and controlled in terms of pollution control measures. The study also says Nanjido landfill covered 2,720,000 square metres, roughly the same as Yeouido Island, and that the low-lying fill reached 13 metres above sea level at its highest point in December 1985.Thereafter, the Nanjido landfill site was divided into two parts named Noeul Park and Haneul Park, as documented in Seoul Solutionâs official record of the landfill recovery project. Initially, officials set a 45-metre height limit in line with international standards for sanitary landfill sites. However, due to delays in the construction of the new site at Gimpo, Seoul had to continue filling the site with more waste and ended up with the creation of two high mounds, each of a height of 92 to 98 metres high, storing nearly 92 million cubic metres of waste. Living conditions at the dump were so poor that it was dubbed âSamdado,â or the island of three excesses: dust, smell and flies. Almost 3,000 people collected trash there for a living, recycling paper, bottles and cans, but gas from decomposition caused about 1,390 fires during the dumpâs 15 years of operation.1998 to 2002: Impermeable barriers, leachate treatment and 106 gas wellsSeoul closed Nanjido to new waste in March 1993 and turned its attention to containing the damage already done. The stabilization project formally began in January 1998 and was completed in October 2002, a span of nearly five years. It included impermeable walls to keep leachate from seeping into local groundwater, leachate management, methane gas extraction wells, mound stabilization to reduce the risk of collapse, and a soil cover on both mounds to allow vegetation to grow on top of them. Leachate from the facility had contained a Biological Oxygen Demand of 72 mg/l and a Total Nitrogen concentration of 1,416 mg/l, levels which could contaminate the Han River and its associated groundwaterTo address methane accumulation within the mounds, engineers constructed 106 gas extraction wells distributed evenly across the old landfill at 120-metre intervals. The methane was then used to provide heating for three public sites, including the World Cup Stadium, 40 office buildings, and 16,335 households in surrounding residential areas. The volume of energy extracted from 2002 to 2014 also amounted to almost 43.85 million cubic metres, worth more than 8.7 billion Korean won.Post-capping survey finds exotic species dominating the landfill slopesOnce the mounds were capped, the question became whether anything could grow on ground built entirely from buried rubbish. A vegetation and soil survey, The Plant Community of Nanjido, a Representative Nonsanitary Landfill in South Korea: Implications for Restoration Alternatives, published in Water, Air, & Soil Pollution, set out to answer exactly that. The researchers surveyed the landfill and nearby forest controls with 10 Ã 10 m quadrats, then analysed soil pH, conductivity, organic matter, nutrients, and texture before running canonical correspondence analysis. They found that landfill soils were less acidic and significantly richer in P, Ca and Mg and that the slopes were already dominated by tree species such as Salix babylonica, Robinia pseudoacacia and Ailanthus altissima.Tree species that had taken hold on their own included willow, plane trees, black locust, tree of heaven and Korean forsythia, while Mongolian oak, the region's natural late-successional species, was largely absent from the disturbed ground. The study found that invasive and exotic plants were more common where disturbance was greater, soil conditions differed, and more exotic species were already present. The authors recommended introducing native plant stock from similar disturbed sites and limiting further ground disturbance as the more realistic path toward a stable, native-dominated cover.May 2002: Opening of five parks on the former landfill siteAhead of the Korea-Japan World Cup, the parks opened to the public in May 2002, several months before the broader landfill stabilization project was formally completed in October 2002 The five parks make up World Cup Park, built on the former landfill site and adjacent land. Haneul Park and Noeul Park are located on top of the two old garbage heaps, whereas Pyeonghwa Park and Nanjicheon Park are found on the flattened reclaimed land and Nanji Hangang Park is found along the riverside.The project is widely known internationally. According to Seoul Solution, the city received a Special Award from UN-HABITAT and attracts about 3,000 visitors a year from other countries who come to learn about the project. What began as a last-resort response to a waste problem became a 24-year lesson in restoring heavily polluted land. Methane is still being monitored beneath the turf at Haneul Park, showing that the landfill remains active beneath the surface.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. Download the TOI app.

articles.title: Massive floods sweep through Nepal; several districts put on high alert
articles.summary: South Asia News: At least eight people were killed and several others are missing after a sudden cloudburst triggered a sharp rise in the Bhotekoshi River, causing wid.
articles.body: At least eight people were killed and several others are missing after a sudden cloudburst triggered a sharp rise in the Bhotekoshi River, causing widespread flooding in Nepalâs Rasuwa district near the China border on Wednesday.Across the border in Tibet, the flooding also reportedly caused âmajor casualtiesâ, according to Chinese state media.The areas of Timure and Syafrubesi were among those badly affected, with vehicles, goods and other property washed away.âA sudden flood in Rasuwa has caused damage to the market area, including Syaprubesi. Initial reports have come that the flood that has been occurring for some time has caused great damage to the settlement and market area. The exact details of the flood damage have not yet been received,â said Narendra Pariyar, chief district officer of Rasuwa.The floodwater reportedly came from the direction of Tibet and surged through the Bhote Koshi River around 9 am local time.The Nepal army said the sudden rise in water caused widespread destruction in Timure and the nearby Syafrubesi area. Vehicles, goods and other property were swept away.Rasuwa district is located northeast of Kathmandu, around 125 km from the Tibet border.High alert in several districtsThe National Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Authority (NDRRM) has asked people living near river banks in Rasuwa, Nuwakot, Dhading, Chitwan and Gorkha to remain on high alert and take necessary safety measures until further notice.Rasuwa assistant chief district officer Dhruva Prasad Adhikari said the scale of the flooding was unusually large and that the two settlements had suffered significant damage.Rasuwa chief customs officer Rajendra Dhungana said several vehicles and goods kept at the customs premises were swept away. A recently constructed bridge was also destroyed.Rescue operations under wayThe Nepal Prime Ministerâs Office said personnel from the Nepal army, armed police force and Nepal Police had been deployed in Rasuwa and nearby areas to strengthen rescue and relief operations.A high-level meeting will also be held to assess the situation and decide on further measures, according to the PMâs Office.The Nepal army has sent two helicopters to areas near the Trishuli River for search and rescue operations. An MI-17 helicopter equipped with an Emergency Medical Rescue Team has also been sent towards the district hospital in Trishuli, the army said.The army said details of the damage were still being collected and the full extent of the destruction was not yet known.Not caused by rainfallAccording to Nepalâs department of hydrology and meteorology, Wednesdayâs flooding was not caused by rainfall in Rasuwa.The development comes a year after two catastrophic floods hit the Bhotekoshi River in Rasuwa, killing at least 10 people.That flooding was caused by the sudden draining of a previously unnoticed âsupraglacialâ lake.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.body:
Christian Gonzalez has been speaking to the media about his contract talks with the New England Patriots this week.

At present, Gonzalez is on a 4-year rookie contract worth $15.1 million with the Patriots. That deal is said to run through the 2026 season with the option of an extension in 2027.

There has been much talk about the Patriots star getting a new deal, but at present, he is yet to pen fresh terms.

Christian Gonzalez frustrated over New England Patriots contract talks

Gonzalez is now back in training with the Patriots ahead of the new season getting underway following an injury problem.

Now, he has spoken about his contract situation ahead of their next pre-season match against the Cleveland Browns .

When doing so, as per the New York Post , Gonzalez initially said: "I'm not going to get into that. I'm out here now. So it is what it is."

However, he then went on to express his frustration at the situation, saying: "It's frustrating. But I'm focused on the season. I'm focused on here now and doing what I have to do. I'm out here to compete and get better."

The Patriots take on the Cleveland Browns on Thursday evening in what will be their final pre-season match.

They will then kick off their proper campaign on September 9 against the Seattle Seahawks .

articles.title: Savannah audited 39,000 Flock searches and found 34 unjustified; 6 employees were fired and 4 have now been arrested
articles.summary: US News: Four former Savannah Police Department employees were arrested on Friday after an investigation into the alleged misuse of the Flock Safety license pl.
articles.body: Four former Savannah Police Department employees were arrested on Friday after an investigation into the alleged misuse of the Flock Safety license plate reader system.The former employees have been booked into the Chatham County Jail, local broadcaster WTOC reported. Out of them, three are former police officers, while the fourth worked as a community service specialist. All four had been fired from the Savannah Police Department earlier in August.It all started with internal investigation by the Savannah Police Department on July 27. Two days later, the department asked the Georgia Bureau of Investigation (GBI) to look into the case.The internal audit examined 39,000 Flock searches made so far this year. Of those, 127 searches were flagged for review. The police department determined that 34 of the searches were unjustified. Six employees were ultimately fired, although only four have been arrested so far.Flock searches on family, acquaintances The four arrested employees are 48-year-old Marquis Dillard, 23-year-old Donald Phillips, 39-year-old Matthew Rich and 34-year-old Calandic Thomas.Dillard, Phillips and Rich are former officers. Each faces two counts of misuse of a license plate reader system and two counts of violation of oath of office. Thomas, a former community service specialist, faces two counts of misuse of a license plate reader system.According to the City of Savannah, Dillard spent 10 years with the Savannah Police Department and most recently worked as a homicide detective before his termination. Phillips had worked for the department for two-and-a-half years. Rich served with the department for 13 years before he was fired. Thomas worked as a community service specialist for just under three years.The four former employees are accused of running Flock license plate searches on personal acquaintances and family members. One of the officers is also accused of giving an outside agency unauthorised access to the system.The GBI confirmed that the outside agency is also part of its investigation. However, it has not identified the agency.Flock license plate reader systems allow law enforcement agencies to search information collected by cameras. Savannah has 106 Flock cameras, and Georgia has the second-most Flock cameras of any state in the US.'Breach of public trust'Savannah Mayor Van Johnson criticised the alleged misuse of the technology and the breach of public trust.âWe entrusted these individuals with advanced technology, and even more importantly, with the publicâs trust,â Johnson said. âNobody is above the law, and everyone trusted with public confidence is accountable,â he added, as quoted by WTOC.Police Chief Lenny Gunther also said department employees must follow the law and maintain professional standards.âThe actions of a few do not reflect the dedication and professionalism of the men and women who honorably serve our community every day,â Gunther said.Gunther said he is working to introduce a formal policy governing the use of Flock cameras. The department also plans to conduct weekly inspections using its audit-assist tool to identify possible misuse earlier.Flock technology faces scrutinyThe Savannah case has added to wider concerns about how automated license plate reader systems are used and monitored.Police departments say the technology can help investigators locate missing people, recover stolen vehicles and investigate serious crimes. However, the systems have also raised questions about privacy, data access and how information collected by the cameras is shared.CBS News reported that the Savannah arrests are part of a growing list of alleged misuse cases involving automated license plate readers in Georgia. In July, five former Albany police officers were arrested after an internal audit found they had accessed retained Flock license plate data for non-law-enforcement purposes.Georgia already has rules governing license plate data held by law enforcement agencies. Under state law, such data can be accessed only for a law enforcement purpose. Agencies can share the information with other law enforcement agencies for those purposes.The law also requires agencies using automated license plate recognition systems to maintain policies governing their use and officer training. Knowingly obtaining or using the data under false pretences or for another purpose can result in a misdemeanor of a high and aggravated nature.Flock Safety has also announced changes to its safeguards. CEO Garrett Langley said the company is moving towards a seven-day default retention period for license plate reader data, down from 30 days. Evidence connected to active investigations can still be preserved.The company also says law enforcement customers will be required to use its Audit Assistance system, which is designed to flag unusual search activity. Other changes include requiring case codes for searches and automatically suspending access in some situations until suspicious activity can be reviewed. âWe're setting a higher bar for ourselves and the industry,â Langley said.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: Hawaii mixed recycled fishing nets into an Oahu road; 11 months later, researchers found no more polyethylene microplastics than in regular asphalt
articles.summary: US News: Hawaii is addressing its plastic waste crisis by melting recycled fishing gear into asphalt, revealing insights on microplastics in roads after an 11-month test.
articles.body: Shipping waste off HawaiÊ»i's islands is expensive, local landfills are running out of room, and Pacific currents keep depositing tons of derelict fishing gear onto the shoreline. Researchers at HawaiÊ»i Pacific University tested whether washed-up plastic could be melted into asphalt and returned about 11 months later to test whether the road was shedding microplastics back into the environment.Derelict fishing gear becomes HawaiÊ»i's largest marine debris problemJennifer Lynch, director of CMDR at HawaiÊ»i Pacific University, says most debris in Hawaiian waters consists of fishing nets and fishing lines that drift in from elsewhere. HawaiÊ»i has been adopting polymer-modified asphalt since around 2020 for its improved resistance to cracking, rutting and water damage in the state's tropical climate. That pavement is normally made by melting a virgin plastic copolymer into the asphalt binder before it is mixed with heated rock and sand.However, the HawaiÊ»i Department of Transportation wondered if some of that virgin plastic could be replaced by recycled plastic, such as the abandoned fishing equipment that was being washed ashore on the beaches of the island state. The agency asked Lynch's group to supply fishing nets for the asphalt mix and to determine whether the asphalt would shed more microplastics than regular asphalt.CMDR's Bounty Project removes tons of fishing gear from the Pacific CMDR has implemented an initiative known as the Bounty Program, whereby commercial licensed fishermen are rewarded for retrieving lost fishing equipment, according to HawaiÊ»i Pacific Universityâs announcement of the project. As of the study's presentation in March 2026, HawaiÊ»i Pacific University reported the initiative had retrieved 84 tons of large fishing equipment from the Pacific. articles.title: Keenan Allen changed Ashton Dulin's role. Now the Colts may use him everywhere.
articles.summary: Veteran Ashton Dulin has been the Colts' No. 2 healthy receiver in training game but may drop to No. 4, opening up roles on special teams.
articles.body:
Brian Mason has never been shy in his views of Ashton Dulin 's performance on special teams, calling the 29-year-old receiver veteran "one of the three-best special teams players in the NFL" last fall.

How much the Colts will be able to take advantage of those skills – on his most active days, Indianapolis uses his 4.4 speed as its primary gunner on punt coverage, as well as one of its two returners on kickoffs – may vary week-to-week, depending on the team's health across the board.

After last week's signing of six-time Pro Bowl receiver Keenan Allen , Dulin finds himself no longer in contention for one of the Colts ' three starting wideout spots. Instead he's jockeying with Nick Westbrook-Ikhine for fourth on the depth chart on a team whose star second-year tight end Tyler Warren makes Dulin or Westbrook-Ikhine the fifth receiving option at-best.

NFL preseason; Indianapolis Colts against Atlanta Falcons

Dulin has performed arguably the most consistently of Indianapolis' rotational wideouts in the preseason, all while taking very few reps on special teams. It gave the appearance the Colts planned to significantly reduce his role on punt and kick teams to preserve his energy and impact for offense. But with Allen's signing dropping Dulin a spot, the receiver who has just seven catches since the end of the 2022 campaign finds himself in virtually the same spot as the end of last season.

"How many phases and plays he gets on special teams will just be dictated by how many plays (the offensive coaches) anticipate him getting in a game," Colts special teams coordinator Brian Mason told reporters Monday. "We usually meet at the beginning of a regular season game week, and we'll kinda project who'll be up for the week and how much they plan to play.

"If they say, 'He's going to play this number of plays' on offense, that will then determine whether he plays in one, two or three phases on special teams."

As Mason went on to explain, the Colts plan to look at Dulin as a potential punt returner this week, among a long list of kick return spots. Among players in the NFL in 2025 with more than one kickoff return attempt, Dulin's 32.3-yard average ranked third-best in the league, but in the background, Mason said Dulin has been working on his punt return skills for two years.

Through two preseason games, second-year receiver Coleman Owen has been the Colts' most consistent and active returner on kicks and punts, with rookie running back Seth McGowan and rookie receiver Deion Burks , shuffling through in preseason action. Incumbent starting returner Anthony Gould has been out for much of camp with a groin injury, while the team lost frequent returner Ameer Abdullah in free agency. Josh Downs has taken reps on punt return, but the team would like to limit that given his increasing role in the offense.

Mason went on to explain that Dulin's lack of special teams reps throughout training camp came, in part, so the team could evaluate its young fringe roster players to narrow in on final contenders for various roles he would be a finalist for, pending his responsibilities on offense.

"We planned on using Ashton Dulin in roles no matter what, whether that be on kick return or at gunner. If he ever needs a sub at gunner, we can always give him a sub, but we certainly still want to have the threat of being able to use him and our opponent knowing there's a good chance he still may be out there," Mason said. "I think that does affect certain people's punt return game plan.

"If Ashton Dulin is on the field for the punt team, you certainly have to account for him and you certainly need to probably (double-team) him in order to prevent him from causing problems."

articles.title: ‘Made it easy’ – Carlos Alcaraz praises Serena Williams after US Open mixed doubles appearance
articles.summary: Carlos Alcaraz and Serena Williams crashed out of US Open mixed doubles, but not before getting an impressive win. Alcaraz had great things to say about the...
articles.body:
Carlos Alcaraz and Serena Williams crashed out of US Open mixed doubles, but not before getting an impressive win. Alcaraz had great things to say about the legendary Williams after their victory.

The US Open mixed doubles event has seen some glamorous pairings. Aryna Sabalenka and Novak Djokovic participated, and Carlos Alcaraz played alongside Serena Williams.

Sabalenka and Djokovic faced an upset in the first round, but Williams and Alcaraz managed to make it all the way to the quarter-finals.

They recorded a win against Lloyd Glasspool and Erin Routliffe in the Round of 16 before succumbing to Flavio Cobolli and Belinda Bencic in the quarter-finals.

Carlos Alcaraz says Serena Williams helped him with his nervousness in mixed doubles game

The duo won their game in the Round of 16 with a score of 5-3 and 4-1. After a tough first set, they got the job done with ease in the second.

Alcaraz is playing for the first time since his wrist injury in April kept him out of multiple major tournaments this year. And he praised Williams for being a calming presence for him.

"Everyone could see how nervous I was," Alcaraz said. "I made a double fault on the first point. I was really, really nervous….

"I was out for almost five months. I almost forgot how it felt to step on court once again. (The nervousness) was just for a couple of games, then Serena made it easy for me."

The duo may be out of the tournament already, but they drew a lot of attention with their performance. Now all eyes will be on Alcaraz to see how the Spaniard plays when the men's singles begin.

articles.title: Arsenal verbally agree club-record £56.5m sale
articles.summary: Al Hilal and Arsenal have reached a verbal agreement for the club-record transfer of Gabriel Martinelli, according to reports.Photo by Alex Pantling/Getty Im...
articles.body:
Al Hilal and Arsenal have reached a verbal agreement for the club-record transfer of Gabriel Martinelli , according to reports.

James Benge of CBS Sports reported on Tuesday that Al Hilal and Arsenal were closing in on an agreement for the transfer of Gabriel Martinelli , with the fee expected to be around €58m (£49.7m) guaranteed, with €8m (£6.9m) in further bonuses.

The total package of £56.5m would represent a club-record sale for Arsenal, but Benge added that it's all subject to the player's final approval.

Sami Mokbel then confirmed for the BBC that Arsenal are closing in on a minimum £50m deal to sell Martinelli, with talks advanced and a conclusion imminent ahead of the winger making a formal decision.

Tom Canton reports for Football.London that a sell-on clause in the deal is one of many aspects of the deal being finalised in the last 24 hours, with Benge also previously reporting that the Gunners were looking to include such a clause in the deal.

Fabrizio Romano writes this morning that the player's agent is in direct contact with Al Hilal to seal an agreement on personal terms.

Romano confirms that a package worth over €65m has been verbally agreed between the two clubs, so it's all up to the player now.

Martinelli has been a key player for Arsenal over the last seven years, making 278 appearances and scoring 62 goals from his spot on the left wing.

The 25-year-old has won the Premier League, the FA Cup, and the Community Shield, and he extended his contract on a couple of occasions amid intense interest from elsewhere.

But the last couple of weeks have made it clear Mikel Arteta no longer intends to give the winger significant minutes, leaving him out of the matchday squads against Manchester City and Coventry City . It seems he's now on the verge of a move to the Saudi Pro League.

articles.title: Oil prices fall $2 on Iran-Oman talks to reopen Strait of Hormuz
articles.summary: By Anushree Mukherjee Aug 26 (Reuters) - Oil prices fell more than $2 a barrel to a two-week low on Wednesday as talks between Iran and Oman revived hopes th...
articles.body:
Aug 26 (Reuters) - Oil prices fell more than $2 a barrel to a two-week low on Wednesday as talks between Iran and Oman revived hopes that the Strait ‌of Hormuz could reopen and remove shipping constraints affecting supply in the key Middle ‌East region.

Brent crude futures fell $2.25, or 2.54%, to $86.33 a barrel by 0810 GMT, earlier dropping to their lowest since August 13. ​U.S. West Texas Intermediate crude futures were down $2.21, or 2.68%, at $80.15, earlier sinking to their lowest since August 10.

"It's renewed focus on the discussion between Iran and Oman regarding a deal for transiting oil and other petrochemicals through the Strait of Hormuz. So that sort of creates some optimism," said Bjarne Schieldrop, chief ‌analyst, commodities, at SEB Research.

Iran said ⁠it had restarted talks with Oman to manage the strait as it faces heightened economic pressure from U.S. President Donald Trump.

The two countries have held intermittent discussions ⁠for weeks over oversight of the vital waterway, which carried about a fifth of global oil and liquefied natural gas shipments before the U.S.-Israeli war with Iran began in February.

The two countries said on Tuesday that ​they discussed "a ​joint temporary navigational corridor" through the strait and agreed ​to clear it of mines.

While the discussions ‌continue, ship traffic through Hormuz remains subdued. Only five commodity vessels transited the waterway on Tuesday, preliminary data from shiptracker Kpler showed, down from the 10-day average of 15 and well below pre-war levels.

Talks on an overall end to the conflict also continue. Pakistan and Iran made "significant progress" in talks that focused on the U.S.-Israeli war on Iran and a path to peace, Pakistan's interior minister said on ‌Tuesday, at the end of a visit to Tehran.

On Monday, ​Washington expanded sanctions aimed at cutting off Iran's economic lifeline, ​threatening to punish countries that continue to ​do business with Tehran, though it said it would not impose penalties immediately.

In ‌the U.S., the American Petroleum Institute reported crude ​oil inventories rose by ​about 4.2 million barrels in the week ended August 21, market sources said.

Analysts polled by Reuters estimated crude oil stockpiles would rise by about 600,000 barrels on average. Official data from ​the EIA, the statistical arm of ‌the U.S. Department of Energy, are due at 10:30 a.m. ET (1430 GMT) on Wednesday.

(Reporting ​by Anushree Mukherjee in Bengaluru, Yuka Obayashi in Tokyo and Siyi Liu in Singapore; ​Editing by Chris Reese, Sonali Paul and Christian Schmollinger)

articles.title: 'Just fantastic with people.' Tom O'Brien had a lifelong connection with Cathedral
articles.summary: Tom O'Brien was coaching at the college level in 1967 when he came back to coach at Cathedral, his alma mater. He maintained longtime connection.
articles.body:
Tom O'Brien was a college basketball assistant at Bradley in 1967 when the opportunity arose to come back to coach at Cathedral, his alma mater.

O'Brien would leave a couple different times as coach, but never really did give up his connection to the school where he graduated from in 1949. O'Brien died on Aug. 17 at age 95.

"Tom had such a history with Cathedral, graduating from there and all the changes the school went through in good times and bad times, Tom was always part of it," said Steve Hodgson, who coached with O'Brien and then later succeeded him. "It goes even beyond that. There are so many families in the Catholic and Eastside community and people that I've heard from in the last week through Tom's passing that he touched."

O'Brien not only coached football, basketball and baseball at Cathedral, he later returned as a substitute and earned the nickname "Super Sub."

"Tom left a profound impact on Cathedral, both as a student and when he returned as an educator and coach," Cathedral shared on its social media accounts. "'Coach OB' coached football, basketball and baseball at Cathedral, leaving a lasting legacy on thousands of Cathedral students. During the final years of his tenure at Cathedral, he was affectionately known as 'Super Sub,' and students were always thrilled to see him walk through the classroom door."

O'Brien, who played football at Butler for legendary coach Tony Hinkle, coached on the staff at Evansville College for Arad McCutchan, helping the Aces to a perfect season in 1964-65. That team was led by Larry Humes and Jerry Sloan. But after coaching at Evansville and Bradley, O'Brien was drawn home with the opportunity to coach basketball at Cathedral.

After leading Cathedral to a 71-27 record over a four-year period, including the program's first sectional championship in 1971, O'Brien also served as the Marion County Clerk from 1975-79 before he was rehired as Cathedral's coach in 1979.

"He was a really, really good coach," said Brad Lennon, who was hired as O'Brien's freshman team coach in 1980 and coached on his staff the next six seasons. "He wasn't necessarily a master technician but he was a players' coach. He had a heart of gold and would do anything for anybody – just fantastic with people."

Steve Hodgson remembered one afternoon when O'Brien was feeling sick and was not going to be able to make it to a game at Center Grove. He spent 45 minutes talking on the phone to Hodgson, his assistant at Cathedral, about the game plan for the night. Just before the tipoff, O'Brien showed up at the game, saying he was "feeling better and coming to support the kids."

"I turned to Brad and said the over/under on him sitting on this bench is halftime," Hodgson said with a laugh. "I missed it by a quarter. If he was there, he was going to coach. I'd probably be the same way."

O'Brien's best team was the 1981-82 group led by senior Ken Barlow and junior Scott Hicks, both of whom would go on to Notre Dame; Shelton Smith (Wisconsin) and Carl Daniels (Rice). Cathedral was 27-2 going into the Final Four but ran into a buzzsaw in Scott Skiles and Plymouth, falling 62-59 in the afternoon game. Plymouth would beat Gary Roosevelt 75-74 in double overtime for the state championship that night.

"It was a tremendous experience for the kids to play in a packed Market Square Arena," Hodgson said. "We were probably the proverbial favorites. I remember in the locker room after the game, Tom talked to the kids about how it was one day in their lives. He told them they had an incredible season and were able to go to the Final Four ... all the great things they accomplished. Even though he was heartbroken and we all were, I appreciated those comments."

O'Brien stepped down in 1984. He coached nine seasons total at Cathedral, compiling a 164-60 record. He would go on to coach at Blackford in 1986 after two years working in the Marion County Sheriff's Department. O'Brien would later be a Sagamore of the Wabash recipient and an inaugural member of the Cathedral Circle of Excellence. On his 80th birthday, Mayor Greg Ballard declared it "Tom O'Brien Day" in Indianapolis.

"I might not have gotten into coaching if it wasn't for OB," Lennon said. "He was really good about letting you have your two cents as an assistant coach. Just a great guy with a great sense of humor. I owe him a lot."

O'Brien is proceeded in death by his wife, Marilyn O'Brien, his parents, five brothers James, Robert, Jack, Michael, Bernard and sisters Mary O'Brien and Patricia Norton. He is survived by his daughters, Dorothy (Pete) Miller, Kathleen Allgood and sister Barbara (Joseph) Minatel as well as many nieces and nephews.

Visitation will be held on Wednesday from 4-8 p.m. at Feeney-Hornak Keystone Mortuary, 2126 E. 71st Street. A Mass of Christian Burial will be held on Thursday at 11 a.m. at St. Lawrence Catholic Church 6944 E. 46th Street, with burial to follow in Westridge Park Cemetery.

Memorial contributions go to Cathedral Tuition Assistance Fund, 5225 E. 56th St., Indianapolis, IN 46226.

Just one year after his move to Manchester City, Omar Marmoush already appears to be on the move again. The Egyptian is reportedly set to join Tottenham in London from the Citizens on loan. That is being reported by 'The Athletic' and Florian Plettenberg alike.

According to Plettenberg, the loan could also become an obligation to buy under certain circumstances. If that clause is triggered, Spurs would likely have to send £50 million to Manchester, which is roughly equivalent to €58 million.

Incidentally, Eintracht will not receive any share of the deal, according to matching reports from Plettenberg and Sven Michel.

Reports claiming that Man City had wanted to structure Marmoush's price in a certain way to avoid a sell-on payment to Frankfurt are "nonsense," Plettenberg's side says.

Marmoush is reportedly set to undergo his medical later today before being officially unveiled. As David Ornstein reports, he has already said goodbye to his City teammates.

articles.title: Jaissle set to get his wish with Gonzalez
articles.summary: Although Newcastle's young side came within seconds of defeating Liverpool on the opening weekend, there was always going to be work to do before the window...
articles.body:
Although Newcastle 's young side came within seconds of defeating Liverpool on the opening weekend, there was always going to be work to do before the window shut on 1 September.

Newcastle have made six signings so far this summer in goalkeepers Lukas Hornicek and Ewen Jaouen, defender Amar Dedic, midfielders Aladji Bamba and Sean Steur and forward Bazoumana Toure.

But Matthias Jaissle made it clear that "adjustments need to be done and will be" in an interview with BBC Sport last week.

After reluctantly selling talisman Guimaraes to Arsenal , Nico Gonzalez possesses the qualities Newcastle have been looking for in the middle of the park.

This is a player who would have been potentially out of reach not so long ago.

Of those midfielders who played a minimum of 900 minutes in Europe's top five leagues last season, Gonzalez led the way for high turnovers per game (2.13).

He also ranked in the Premier League's top five midfielders for line-breaking passes per match (12).

Those traits - in and out of possession - could make Gonzalez an invaluable addition as he is handed a greater role at St James' Park.

articles.title: In 1998, Israel closed the Hiriya landfill after decades of waste had formed a 60-metre mound; years later, methane wells, trees and trails helped transform the site into the centrepiece of a 2,000-acre park
articles.summary: Rest of World News: Discover how the former Hiriya landfill in Israel evolved into the lush Ariel Sharon Park, a prime example of urban reclamation and sustainable design, transforming environmental hazards into a thriving green space.
articles.body: In August 1998, Israel closed the Hiriya landfill after almost five decades of receiving waste from the Dan Region. By then, the site had grown into a garbage hill of roughly 60 metres high. This huge landfill footprint accounted for an estimated 25 million tons of accumulated waste, a figure supported by a 2006 peer-reviewed study that calculated the physical volume of the buried material at approximately 16 million cubic metres. The landfillâs closure, however, did not remove the mountain; instead, it began a long process of engineering, gas management and landscape rehabilitation that eventually led to the former dump becoming the centrepiece of Ariel Sharon Park, a planned metropolitan park covering about 2,000 acres.An accumulating waste mountain turns into an environmental hazardHiriya opened in 1952 and became the principal waste-disposal ground for most of the Dan Region. According to O. Ayalon, N. Becker and E. Shaniâs 2006 study published in Waste Management, the landfill operated until 1998 and developed into a major environmental hazard. When the site closed, approximately 16 million cubic metres of waste were estimated to remain buried there. The study also identified several problems requiring rehabilitation, including greenhouse gas emissions, unstable slopes and leachate formation.The moundâs location made things even more complicated, with the landfillâs proximity to Ben Gurion Airport and the birds attracted by decomposing waste. Contemporary accounts identified those birds as an aviation hazard because of their proximity to aircraft during takeoff and landing. However, the bird problem was only one part of a larger environmental challenge that included leachate, landfill gas, instability and the sheer scale of the waste mound.The 2006 study pointed out that closing the landfill did not mean simply walking away from it. While emergency interim measures were deployed immediately in 1998 to manage urgent bird hazards and slope stability, comprehensive, long-term rehabilitation efforts began in 2001, including site investigations, engineering and scientific evaluations and planning for the landscapeâs eventual use. The conclusion notes that engineering rehabilitation was necessary to make a public park possible, while converting the site into a park provided the strongest justification for the wider reclamation attempt.Methane wells help stabilise the waste mountainOne of the most persistent problems faced by the authorities was the landfill gas. Organic material buried in the mountain continued to decompose after the landfill stopped accepting waste, producing methane. As per Hiriyaâs current account of its biogas project, to address this, an engineered gas-extraction system was developed to draw methane from the mass of waste, eventually expanding to comprise approximately 100 wells divided into nine clusters. These wells were drilled to depths of about 12 to 27 metres, depending on local leachate levels.Hiriyaâs records indicate that the gas project was already developing before the park became a public landscape. An agreement giving Ayalon Biogas the extraction rights was signed in 2005, and by capturing the methane and piping it to a nearby textile factory to replace fossil fuels, the project successfully mitigated greenhouse gas emissions. As a result, in 2006, the initiative received formal registration under the UN Clean Development Mechanism.Meanwhile, planners were still contemplating what the enormous waste mound could be transformed into. In 2004, an international competition was held to find a way to rehabilitate Hiriya and give the former landfill a new identity. Fourteen proposals were submitted, and German landscape architect Peter Latz and his team won the competition. A 2023 peer-reviewed study of the competition describes the winning proposal as turning the waste mountain into a prominent landscape monument while addressing the siteâs polluted past. The park was conceived on a scale much larger than the landfill itself, that is, about 2,000 acres that included the former waste mountain and its surrounding site.Trees and trails replaced the old landscapeThe physical transformation required that the waste mountain be treated as an engineered landform rather than an ordinary hill. Landscape plans called for its surface to be protected with engineered layers and clean soil so vegetation could grow without coming directly in contact with the waste beneath it. This approach allowed trees, grasses and other plants to become a part of the new landscape while the former wasteland continued to be monitored and managed underneath.By the early 2010s, the summit of the past landfill had already acquired landscaped paths and an overlook, while additional cycling and recreation facilities were being developed across the wider park. The Times of Israel reported that the larger park project had been officially approved as a 2,000-acre park and was being built in stages.Therefore, Ariel Sharon Park is often cited as an example of circular urban engineering and landscape reclamation. By capping the waste mass, capturing toxic off-gases, and restoring native flora, planners converted a toxic regional liability into a thriving urban sanctuary. Hiriya's legacy illustrates that modern metropolitan growth does not have to be permanently bound by its past waste, paving the way for sustainable city infrastructure worldwide.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: What would Marmoush give Spurs?
articles.summary: Omar Marmoush is primarily a number nine, but he has rarely been confined to one role across the front line.  Manchester City have followed a similar pattern...
articles.body:
Omar Marmoush is primarily a number nine, but he has rarely been confined to one role across the front line.

At Frankfurt, he was used predominantly through the middle but also appeared as a second striker and from the left. Manchester City have followed a similar pattern, using him mainly as a central attacker while also deploying him from the flank and just behind another forward.

That flexibility could suit Roberto de Zerbi. His teams have often relied on forwards changing positions, dropping towards the ball and then attacking the space created when opponents are drawn out. Marmoush is comfortable doing both.

Former Manchester City defender Nedum Onuoha sees the Egyptian as most dangerous when he is able to threaten the space beyond the defence.

"As much as he is good dropping towards the ball, I think he is better when he plays on the shoulder," he said.

"He needs to be in a team that will constantly play balls in behind and force the opposition to run back towards their own goal. That's when you see a better version of Marmoush."

Opta's Premier League numbers from last season show he averaged 11.46 runs in behind per 90 minutes, almost identical to Dominic Solanke 's 11.61 and ahead of Richarlison 's 10.03. But he also offered considerably more with the ball.

articles.title: Bills overlooked defensive back making a strong preseason impression
articles.summary: Second-year defensive back Jordan Hancock is giving Bills defensive coordinator Jim Leonhard plenty to evaluate because of his versatility.
articles.body:
ORCHARD PARK - Given how the Buffalo Bills brought so many new players into their defensive secondary, both via the draft and free agency, it almost felt like Jordan Hancock was a forgotten man.

Contributing to that dynamic is that it was a bit of out of sight, out of mind for Hancock during the spring because in addition to the arrivals of free agents CJ Gardner-Johnson , Geno Stone , and Dee Alford , and draft picks Davison Igbinosun , Jalon Kilgore and Toriano Pride joining the team, Hancock missed all of the on-field portions of the offseason program recovering from shoulder surgery.

But through this point in training camp and the first two preseason games, if anyone truly had forgotten about the 2025 fifth-round pick , he's reminding everyone exactly who he is.

"It's cool to see because it's a guy who didn't get an offseason at all and, in a new system, that's really hard," coach Joe Brady said. "It's good to see a guy coming off an injury, there's no hesitation, flying around, making plays. He's figuring out what that niche is, and we're asking a lot of him, moving him around. Our nickel plays a lot of different roles, so to be able to play safety, play nickel, help on special teams. It was cool to see him finally make some plays."

A delayed start but fast climb for Jordan Hancock

Through the first two preseason games according to Pro Football Focus charting, Hancock has played 57 total snaps, 38 of those as a slot corner and 17 at free safety, plus two random snaps on the line. He's been in on five tackles and every one of them was regarded as a "stop" which PFF defines as a tackle that caused a failure for the offense. Although he has allowed five receptions on six targets, those have gone for just 12 yards total.

"I told you he was going to be one of the biggest evaluations this camp because he did miss the offseason," defensive coordinator Jim Leonhard said. "Any time you have guys who missed snaps on the field, you have to play a little bit of catch up as far as the evaluation and he's doing a great job.

"It's finding the right amount of snaps, the right roles for him. Obviously he has to be a little bit of a Swiss Army knife right now as far as learning safety, learning the nickel position. There are other sub grouping packages that we can get him in and do different things that are kind of that hybrid type of role as well. He's handling it well."

Why versatility matters in Jim Leonhard's defense

Hancock was not a factor in the first half of 2025 but he started getting playing time in the blowout Week 8 victory over Carolina and was active for every game thereafter with the exception of Week 17 against the Eagles and the divisional round playoff loss to the Broncos .

He played 398 total snaps, including special teams. Of those, 183 came on defense, with most of that work at free safety and only six snaps in the slot. This year in Leonhard's defense, the slot corner will be deployed differently than it was over the last several seasons when Taron Johnson occupied the role on nearly every snap.

Leonhard is going to play matchups and will use Alford as the primary starter, but he will rotate others in depending on who lines up across that position, and Hancock could be in the mix.

"It helps a lot," Hancock said of being versatile. "I planted my seed last year and was growing and growing every day with both positions being versatile. I feel like I just got on the field, I played more than I was expected to play. I had opportunities, whether I made the play or not, I had the opportunity to be out there. Now to be in a position where I have to play either position, safety or nickel, I'm trying to be the best at both spots for sure."

The 6-foot, 195-pounder is a dynamic athlete. Basketball was his first love growing up outside Atlanta - his favorite player was Russell Westbrook - and he could dunk a basketball when he stood just 5-foot-7 as an eighth grader, though he could just as easily drop a bomb from three-point range.

It was Mel Tucker, who was the defensive coordinator at Georgia and later the head coach at Michigan State, who after seeing him at football practice while on the recruiting trail told Hancock that football should be his primary sport.

That didn't pay off for Tucker because Ohio State swooped in and signed Hancock and he went on to play 42 games for the Buckeyes totaling 98 tackles, 2.5 sacks, three interceptions, 14 passes defensed and four forced fumbles.

"Just being at Ohio State, just being around great people, great coaches," he said regarding his pedigree playing in a big-time program and how that helped his transition to the NFL. "You're not bigger than anybody. There's always room for improvement and I feel like that's with me, I feel like improvement is a lot. I feel like I can improve and develop, and I'm ready to learn and ready to compete."

Bills looking for answers beyond the starters

In addition to being a physical player, Hancock has the ability to quickly diagnose what's happening, though he does have a tendency to play almost too fast and it gets him out of position. Often, he can recover, but occasionally he doesn't and especially at safety, that can be dangerous.

"He's a confident player," Leonhard said of the former Ohio State standout who played for the Buckeyes' 2024 national championship team. "He's going to make quick decisions and play fast, he's going to make mistakes. There are things that aren't always clean, but he makes fast decisions and he's going to live with the results. You respect that as a coach. You have to take some of the hard edges off sometimes, but you do know he's going to impact the game and he's going to fly around and he's going to set the tone."

Unless there are injuries, Hancock isn't going to be a starter for Buffalo, but if he continues to play the way he has this summer, he's going to get a game-day jersey.

"Every game you get into and there's a situation that pops up where you're one injury or you're one guy having a bad performance away from a lot of pieces moving around," Leonhard said.

"That's always the fun part of being a coach in the NFL is you only have a limited amount of bodies. You get into games and sometimes there's a guy backing up multiple positions and how you're going to play that out and making adjustments, maybe something you thought was going to work well going into the game, you're not getting production out of it and you have to make adjustments. It's huge for me having a handful of guys you know have a flexible skill set. The more players you have in different groups like that, the better."

Sal Maiorana has covered the Buffalo Bills for more than four decades including 37 years as the full-time beat writer/columnist for the D&C. He has written numerous books about the history of the team, and he is also co-host of the BLEAV in Bills podcast/YouTube show. articles.title: Ohio construction workers found a kitten trapped inside an excavator; now she has her own hard hat and a job working with them
articles.summary: US News: A routine day at a construction site in Barberton, Ohio, turned into an unexpected animal rescue when workers discovered a tiny kitten trapped inside .
articles.body: A routine day at a construction site in Barberton, Ohio, turned into an unexpected animal rescue when workers discovered a tiny kitten trapped inside an excavator. The crew at River Reach Construction heard persistent meowing coming from a Komatsu machine and soon realised that the cries were coming from somewhere inside the heavy equipment. Supervisor Chase Guello investigated and helped free the kitten after removing the excavatorâs skid plate. The tiny rescue was later named Sue and quickly became part of the construction crewâs story. What makes the tale even more adorable is what happened next. Sue was given a tiny high-visibility vest and a miniature hard hat, transforming the rescued kitten into the construction companyâs unofficial mascot.Ohio construction workers find kitten trapped inside an excavatorThe unusual rescue began when workers at River Reach Construction heard a kitten crying from inside one of their excavators. The sound was coming from somewhere within the heavy machinery rather than from around the construction site, prompting supervisor Chase Guello to investigate. He eventually discovered the tiny kitten hiding inside the Komatsu excavator. Workers carefully removed the machineâs skid plate, allowing them to reach the animal and get her out safely. The rescue was filmed and later shared online, where the sight of a tiny kitten emerging from a huge piece of construction equipment quickly captured peopleâs attention. For the workers, however, the priority was simply getting the frightened animal out of the machinery without hurting her.The tiny kitten was named Sue after the rescueOnce the kitten was safely out of the excavator, the workers gave her the name Sue as a playful reference to the Komatsu machine in which she had been found. The crew could not locate her mother following the rescue, so Sue was placed with a foster family where she could receive care while recovering. Although she was no longer living inside the construction machinery, the workers who rescued her continued to follow her progress. What started as an unexpected discovery at a worksite soon developed into a much more heartwarming story, with the crew becoming attached to the tiny kitten they had pulled from the excavator.Sue is set to become the construction companyâs shop catSueâs connection with the construction crew did not end with her rescue. River Reach Construction decided to keep her as part of the companyâs extended family, with plans for her to become the shop cat. Local reporting said she will be cared for by shop mechanic Jared and his family. That means the kitten has effectively gone from an unexpected stowaway inside a piece of heavy machinery to a permanent member of the construction companyâs world. While calling her a worker is clearly playful, Sue now has something resembling an official role at the company, giving the tiny rescue an unusually happy ending.The rescued kitten even received her own hard hatSueâs new status came with some remarkably appropriate accessories. Following the attention generated by her rescue, the kitten received a miniature high-visibility vest and a tiny hard hat. The hard hat was made with openings that allow her ears to fit through, making the little construction outfit even more adorable. Photos of Sue wearing the gear helped turn her into the perfect mascot for a construction company. She may not be capable of operating an excavator or carrying out actual construction work, but she certainly looks the part of the crewâs smallest member.Her rescue story quickly captured attention onlineRiver Reach Construction shared footage and updates about Sue on social media, helping the unusual rescue reach audiences far beyond the Ohio construction site. Viewers were particularly drawn to the contrast between the enormous excavator and the tiny kitten that had somehow ended up inside it. The story also prompted plenty of playful reactions, with people online joking about Sue receiving her own hard hat and effectively becoming the crewâs newest employee. The attention has given the construction workersâ unexpected rescue a life far beyond the original incident and turned Sue into a memorable internet mascot.From excavator stowaway to construction mascotSueâs journey is remarkable because of how quickly her circumstances changed. She went from being a vulnerable kitten trapped inside heavy machinery to receiving care from a foster family and eventually finding a permanent place connected to the construction crew that rescued her. Her tiny safety vest and hard hat are clearly more about fun than function, but they perfectly capture the affection the workers have developed for her. What could have ended as a dangerous incident involving an animal trapped inside an excavator instead became a heartwarming rescue story. Now Sue has a safe future, a family to care for her and perhaps the most unusual job title on the construction site, the crewâs tiny shop cat.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: The wit and wisdom of Dolly Parton: 'If you want the rainbow, you gotta put up with the rain'
articles.summary: The much-loved country singer-songwriter in her own words, following her death aged 80.
articles.body:
Dolly Parton, the much-loved US singer-songwriter who has died at the age of 80 , was known for her pearls of wisdom and humour as well as her music.

She regularly offered her perceptive and witty insights about life, music, fame and equal rights.

Here are some of her most memorable quotes from down the years:

"The way I see it, if you want the rainbow, you gotta put up with the rain."

"I always just thought if you see somebody without a smile, give 'em yours!"

"I'm not going to limit myself just because people won't accept the fact that I can do something else."

"If you don't like the road you're walking, start paving another one."

"Don't get so busy making a living that you forget to make a life."

"Sometimes, what would look like to be my biggest mistakes turn out to be my biggest blessings."

"I actually take my songwriting more serious than anything else I do, so I would say I am a songwriter first."

"It's my way of expressing myself. It's my therapy."

"You have to search for a long time because I've written a lot of songs. But yes, there are pieces of me, of course, in everything I write."

"I have to write and sing. See, that was my first love, and I have to do that forever, however I have to do it."

"I look totally artificial, but I am totally real, as a writer, as a professional, as a human being. A rhinestone shines just as good as a diamond."

"My dream was always to make as many people happy as I could in this life."

"I always count my blessings, more than I count my money. I don't work for money, never did. It was the art, it was the job. I loved the work. And I've done well, and I'm thankful for it."

"I wanted more than to just be a farmer's daughter, even though I'm proud to be [one]. I just wanted pretty things. I wanted money to buy the things I had always been impressed with as a child. I wanted, I guess, to be a star."

How Dolly Parton told her life story through six iconic songs

Dolly Parton: Life of the music legend whose songs touched millions

'I’ll think of you each step of the way' - Taylor Swift leads tributes after Dolly Parton dies aged 80

"If I was trying to describe myself to someone that had never seen me before, I would say, 'Calm down. Don't get scared. It's just me. I know I look totally bizarre and artificial, but I'm totally real inside.'"

"I'm not offended by all the dumb blonde jokes because I know I'm not dumb - and I'm not blonde either."

"It costs a lot of money to look this cheap."

"People always ask me how long it takes to do my hair. I don't know, I'm never there."

"If I see something sagging, bagging and dragging, I'm going to nip it, tuck it, and suck it."

"I don't like to be like everybody else. I've often made the statement that I would never stoop so low as to be fashionable. That's the easiest thing in the world to do."

"I make jokes about it, but it's the truth that I kind of patterned my look after the town tramp. I didn't know what she was, just this woman who was blond and piled her hair up, wore high heels and tight skirts, and, boy, she was the prettiest thing I'd ever seen. Momma used to say, 'Aw, she's just trash', and I thought, 'That's what I want to be when I grow up. Trash.'"

"I'm pretty sharp. I'm not educated and I'm not that intelligent, but I'm smart. They say somebody's street smart. I feel like if I got intelligence, it's just a country smart."

Journalist: "What is the trait you most deplore in yourself?" Dolly: "The fact that sometimes my mouth is a little too big and a little too open and sounds too much like a sailor."

"I'm very real where it counts, and that's inside."

"They say love isn't about two people gazing into each other's eyes, it is about two people gazing outwards in the same direction. I believe this with all my heart."

"I never really tried to hide myself from anybody. I think that's one of the reasons I'm still around, people feel like they know me."

"I don't want to be a star if I have no life."

Speaking more about the book gifting programme for children: "Since I had no kids and my husband was pretty independent, I had freedom. So I think a big part of my success is the fact that I was free to work. And I didn't have children, because I believe that God didn't mean for me to have kids, so everybody's kids could be mine, so I could do things like the Imagination Library."

"I ain't never gonna be old because I ain't got time to be old. I can't stop long enough to grow old. I'm just gonna be the best I can be at whatever age I am."

"When I'm done, I can rest in peace knowing I've done my best. I hope that when my time comes, I'll leave something behind that others can use to lift themselves up."

"When I die, I'll really be getting to live then because I believe that there is a greater place than this".

Journalist: "What would be her funeral song?" Dolly: "I don't know - but I won't be singing it!"

"Yes, I support gay marriage. They have every right to be as miserable as straight people."

"And of course black lives matter. Do we think our little white asses are the only ones that matter? No!"

"I've got transgender people. I've got gays. I've got lesbians. I've got drunks. I've got drug addicts - all within my own family. I know and love them all, and I do not judge."

"It's a good thing I was born a girl, otherwise I'd be a drag queen."

In a letter to young recipients of books from Dolly Parton's Imagination Library: "You and all of your friends are very special. There is no limit to what you can do or how far you can go."

She continued: "Just remember the lessons my family taught me - dream big dreams; learn everything you can learn; and care for all those who care for you. You do all of these things and you can be anyone you want to be.

"You are terrific, and remember... I will always love you."
